chapters.title: Born by a Harbour, Raised in a Chawl

blocks.text: Picture a busy British-run port at the bottom tip of Arabia in the mid-1950s. At a petrol pump, a young man from a small Gujarati village is filling tanks. His name is Dhirajlal Hirachand Ambani, and he is known as Dhirubhai.

The port was Aden, then a British colony, today part of Yemen. Dhirubhai first worked at a pedhi, a small Indian trading firm, and then moved to a job with Shell that began at the petrol pump. A journalist whose own father worked in Aden remembered him as junior gas-station staff at Besse, the biggest trading company in the colony.

photo.caption: Steamer Point, Aden, in 1952: the tower, the club and the port buildings of the colony where Mukesh Ambani was born a few years later.
photo.author: The National Archives UK

blocks.text: Mukesh Dhirubhai Ambani was born in Aden in ==1957==. Decades later, an interviewer asked him how long the family had lived there. His answer was short: "From 1954 to 1957. I was born there." His mother, Kokilaben, was with Dhirubhai in Aden through those years.
The richest man in Asia was born abroad, to a petrol-pump worker.
A village boy who sold bhajias

To understand Mukesh, you have to meet his father first. Dhirubhai grew up in Chorwad, near Junagadh in Saurashtra, the son of a village school teacher. He studied at Bahadur Kanji High School in Junagadh.

While still a schoolboy, Dhirubhai opened a stall at the foot of Mount Girnar, a hill that pilgrims climb. On weekends he sold bhajias, fried snacks, to the pilgrims. He passed his school-leaving exam, the SSC, only on his second try, and then left for Aden with a job recommendation in his pocket.
Stories about his childhood have always inspired us, taught us how to cope with life's vicissitudes.
blocks.who: Mukesh Ambani on his father, Rediff interview with Pritish Nandy, 1998

blocks.text: By the time Mukesh was born, Dhirubhai had saved about ==Rs 50,000==. Mukesh later said that sum "seemed to him, in those days, to be a pretty neat kitty to come back." So the family returned home to Bombay, now Mumbai. Reliance itself dates that return to 1957, while other accounts say 1958.

In Bombay, Dhirubhai went into trading. He teamed up with his second cousin Champaklal Damani, who had also worked in Aden. They imported polyester yarn and exported spices to Yemen. That small trading firm is the seed of what became Reliance.

For example: the Rs 50,000 did not go into a nice flat. The family moved into a one-bedroom home in a crowded chawl, and the money went into the business. __Dhirubhai put his savings into the company, not into comfort.__

photo.caption: Dhirubhai Ambani on an Indian postage stamp issued in 2002, the year he died. He was Mukesh's first and biggest teacher.
photo.author: India Post, Government of India

blocks.text: Seven people, one bedroom, one shared toilet

The chawl was called Jai Hind Estate, in Kabootarkhana, Bhuleshwar. Bhuleshwar is a congested old commercial area of Bombay, packed with traders. The Ambani flat was on the fourth floor, up a flight of 50 to 60 steps, as Mukesh's younger brother Anil later described it.
Inside there was one bedroom. Seven people lived there, counting the grandmother. Anil remembered the bathroom most of all, because it was not theirs alone.
There was a common bathroom and toilet for a hundred families together in the chawl.
blocks.who: Anil Ambani, interview with Vir Sanghvi, 2002

blocks.text: Mukesh does not remember those years as a hardship story. In a TV interview with Simi Garewal, he called Jai Hind Estate his earliest cherished memory, from when he was about four or five. A 2019 report of that interview describes the family as having felt secure and happy there.
His first memory is one crowded room. Not a mansion. Remember that.

There were four children: Mukesh, Anil, and two sisters, Dipti and Nina. Their mother Kokilaben ran the home. Anil later said the job of keeping the children in line fell to her, "who was just a high-school graduate," and he gave her the credit for how the family turned out.
A teacher who taught nothing from textbooks

Here is a detail almost nobody knows. In the mid-1960s, when Mukesh was about seven or eight, Dhirubhai put an advertisement in the newspaper for a teacher. But the ad said the job was non-academic. He did not want a tutor for marks. He wanted someone to widen his children's world.

He interviewed several people and picked Mahendrabhai Vyas, who taught at the New Era School. Vyas came every evening and stayed until about 6:30 or 7. He played hockey and football with the children, took them to watch matches at the Cooperage ground, and rode buses and trains with them all over Bombay.

photo.caption: The Cooperage football ground in south Mumbai, photographed in 2011. As a boy, Mukesh was taken to watch matches here.
photo.author: AroundTheGlobe

blocks.text: A paid teacher just for curiosity. Very important for future parents too!
Sundays belonged to the family. Mukesh remembered his father taking them out to forests and streams. Every year the family went camping and stayed in a village for 10 to 15 days.
However busy he may have been, whatever the pressure, Sunday was for his wife and kids.
blocks.who: Mukesh Ambani on Dhirubhai, MoneyLIFE interview, 2007

blocks.text: Yet Dhirubhai was not a parent who hovered. Mukesh said his father never came to their school, not even once. He cared about the children growing in every direction, but he left the daily details to them and their mother.
There were boundaries, of course, but within those, we were not micro-managed.
The five-rupee rule

As the business grew, the family was no longer short of money. But the children still did not get to spend freely. Anil put it this way: "We had no lack of monetary resources, but we were given sort of goal-oriented finances."

For example: after an outing, their father offered a choice. Either one drink and one snack, or two snacks and no drink. The budget was ==five rupees==, and Anil said it "didn't change for a long time."
Money was there. The lesson was learning to choose.
Two days in the garage

Not every lesson was gentle. Mukesh told Simi Garewal about an evening when guests came to the house. He was 10 or 11, and Anil was 9. Every time their mother brought food out for the guests, the two boys ate it before the guests could.

At first Dhirubhai stayed calm. Mukesh remembered him patiently saying, "OK! Sit down." The boys kept misbehaving. So their father told them they would stay in the garage for the next two days, until they learned to behave.
We really spent two days in the garage on merely water and roti.
blocks.who: Mukesh Ambani, as reported from his interview with Simi Garewal

blocks.text: Meanwhile, the business grew up too

While Mukesh was a small boy, his father's trading firm was turning into a manufacturer. In ==1966==, when Mukesh was about nine, Dhirubhai set up his first textile mill at Naroda, near Ahmedabad. It made polyester cloth sold under the brand Vimal. A visiting World Bank technical team later praised the mill.

Mukesh later explained the bet behind it. His father had studied textiles deeply, learned the difference between fibres, and gambled on polyester when others did not. By the mid-1960s, Mukesh said, Dhirubhai had become the largest polyester trader around, and that was the foundation of Reliance.
Around 1969 the family finally left the chawl. Anil said he was 10 when they moved out, which made Mukesh about 12. The new home was a flat in a building called Usha Kiran.

blocks.text: So by the age of 12, Mukesh had seen two worlds. He had lived in one room with a shared toilet, and he had watched his father build a factory. __He learned early that money is a tool for building, not a prize for showing off.__

blocks.title: Comfort can wait. The business cannot.
blocks.text: Dhirubhai could have moved his family into a better home much sooner. He chose to keep living small and put money into the next machine and the next trade. For a first-time founder, every rupee spent on looking successful is a rupee not spent on becoming successful.

chapters.title: The Boy Who Spent Weekends at the Office

blocks.text: Moving out of the chawl did not mean an easy life. The Ambani children now lived in a bigger flat, but their father's rules came with them. He wanted his sons to know the country they lived in, not just the rooms they lived in.

Anil remembered one trip in the early 1970s, during mango season. Dhirubhai sent the boys to Goa on the steamer from Bombay, and not in a cabin. They travelled on the lower deck, with no reservation, and in Anil's words "everybody was puking." Their father could easily have paid for a plane.

Why mangoes? Anil explained the logic in one line: "the only ways you can get a full box of mangoes is if you travel by the lower deck on the Bombay to Goa steamer." In other words, the hard, crowded route was also the one that got you the prize. It was a small lesson about how ordinary Indians travelled and traded.
Rich kids on the lower deck. He was teaching them India.

The family's habits were simple too. Anil once said people were shocked to learn that neither he nor Mukesh drank or smoked, that both were vegetarian, and that they did not gamble. Anil said the core values their father passed on were being down to earth, humble and very simple.
Two brothers, two memories

Here is something interesting. The two brothers remember their father's time very differently. Mukesh talks about Sundays outdoors and family camping trips. Anil, two years younger, remembered a father who was almost always at work.
I don't think I recall -- during my entire school or college career -- my father spending time with me.
blocks.who: Anil Ambani, interview with Vir Sanghvi, 2002

blocks.text: Both memories can be true. A father can keep Sundays sacred and still be absent the other six days. What Dhirubhai did make clear was what he expected. Anil said his father told them, "I believe you have the brains so you should study hard." Dhirubhai had wanted to study more himself but never had the money.
Same house, same father, different stories. Memory is personal.
Friends for life

At school, Mukesh made a friend who would stay close for the rest of his life. "Anand and I have been friends since the sixth standard," he said, speaking of Anand Jain. Anand later took commerce while Mukesh took science, but the two stayed tight, and decades later Anand was leading big projects for Reliance.

His circle of friends was small and loyal. It included Ajay Parekh, who would go on to run the company Pidilite, and Kiran Manelkar, who became a doctor. Several of these boys ended up at the same college together.
For example: the friend Mukesh made at about age 11 in sixth standard was still working beside him more than 30 years later. __The people you trust at 15 can become the team you build with at 40.__
Weekends at the office

Most teenagers in Bombay spent their weekends at the beach or the cinema. Mukesh spent his at his father's office. Dhirubhai shared his passion for business with his son from early on, and Mukesh soaked it up.
Even when I was in high school, I used to spend long hours at office on weekends.

He was also watching his father's character up close. "Papa was always very responsible and enterprising," Mukesh said in 1998. What stood out most to him was a spirit of adventure. Even decades later, he said, his mother still talked about that spirit in Dhirubhai.

What was he watching? A company that bought, made and sold polyester. Reliance imported polyester and exported spices, and its Naroda mill was turning out Vimal cloth. A teenager at that office could see every part of a business at once: buying raw material, running machines, and selling to customers.
Your first business school can be your parents' work. Watch closely.
The day of the raid

Then came a moment that tested him. When Mukesh was about 16 or 17, around 1973 or 1974, the business was raided by the authorities. His father was away in the United States. Someone in the family had to deal with it.

That someone was the teenager. "I was literally in charge, handling the problem," Mukesh said years later. He did not say in that interview which agency carried out the raid or how it ended, and we have not found a reliable record of it, so we will not guess.
For example: at the age when most Indian students are worrying about Class 11 and 12 exams, Mukesh was the family's point person during a raid, with his father on the other side of the world.
Sixteen. Facing a raid alone. Pressure training started early.
One line from a movie

What do you study when your father's business is cloth? Everyone at home thought the answer was obvious. Vimal was a successful textile brand, so Mukesh would do textile engineering and join the mill.

But a single line from a Hollywood film had stuck in his head. In The Graduate, a young man fresh out of college is handed career advice in one famous line: "There's a great future in plastics." Mukesh said that line "left a mark on my mind." Chemical engineering, he decided, "was supposed to be the future."
I shocked them by saying that I would go to IIT.
blocks.who: Mukesh Ambani, on telling his family he would not study textiles, 2007

blocks.text: He chose science and he chose his college himself. In those days the IIT entrance results came out before the Inter-science exam results, so he cleared the entrance and joined IIT Bombay. Then, a few weeks later, the Inter-science results arrived.

Mukesh did something few students would do. He left IIT Bombay and joined UDCT, the University Department of Chemical Technology in Matunga, where his friends were going. __He picked the place that fit his goal, not the place with the bigger name.__
He walked out of IIT Bombay. Read that again.

blocks.text: Looking back, the teenage years gave Mukesh three things. He knew the business from the inside, because he had spent his weekends in it. He had faced a real crisis before he was an adult. And he had chosen his own path in studies, even when it surprised his family.

blocks.title: Pick your field for where the world is going
blocks.text: Mukesh's family expected textiles because textiles paid the bills. He picked chemical engineering because he believed it was the future, and that bet later turned Reliance from a cloth company into a polyester, petrochemicals and refining giant. When you choose what to study, ask what will matter in 20 years, not just what matters at home today.

UDCT in Matunga was not glamorous. It was a serious, hard-working place for chemistry and chemical engineering. For Mukesh, it was exactly the right room, and on day one he met the teacher who would shape his thinking for life.

That teacher was Professor M. M. Sharma, a chemical engineer. Most professors begin with theory. Mukesh remembered that Sharma began with money: "Prof MM Sharma's first lecture was on how you make money in the chemical business."
A science lecture about making money. That is why it stuck.

The respect never faded. In June 2025, nearly fifty years later, Mukesh went back to the institute, now called the Institute of Chemical Technology, for the launch of a biography of Sharma called Divine Scientist. There he announced an unconditional grant of ==Rs 151 crore== to the institute as guru dakshina, a student's gift to a teacher.
When he tells us something, we just listen. We don't think.
blocks.who: Mukesh Ambani on Professor M. M. Sharma, June 2025

blocks.text: He even compared his teacher to his father. "Like my father Dhirubhai Ambani, he had a burning desire to change Indian industry from scarcity to global leadership," he said. He called Sharma a quiet architect of India's economic reforms.

photo.caption: The Pidilite Pavilion sports hall at the Institute of Chemical Technology in Matunga, Mumbai, the college Mukesh knew as UDCT. Photographed in 2015.
photo.author: Mandarchougule

blocks.text: Find one teacher who changes how you think. Keep them for life.
College also widened his circle. His school friends were around him, and at UDCT he met a new friend, Manoj Modi. It was a small, close group of friends who had chosen the same college together.
A board seat at twenty
Something unusual happened while Mukesh was still a student. Reliance says he has been on its board ==since 1977==. He was about 20 years old.

That same year, Reliance Textile Industries sold shares to the public for the first time. The issue was oversubscribed seven times, which means people asked for seven times more shares than were on offer. Reliance says this IPO helped start the habit of ordinary Indians investing in shares.

That public money left a mark on how Mukesh talks about the company. Among the lessons he took from his father, he listed the idea that the company holds other people's savings in trust. "We have taken money from ordinary Indians and we are their trustees," he said.

blocks.text: Be honest about what this means. A 20-year-old does not usually sit on the board of a listed company. Mukesh got that seat because he was the founder's son. __Family businesses give their children a head start, and the real test is what they do with it.__
Twenty years old and a director. Most of us won't get that.
Stanford and the professor's question

After his engineering degree, Mukesh went to the United States to study business at Stanford University. He found both his classmates and his teachers outstanding. One professor in particular made a big impact on him: Bill Sharpe, a finance professor who later won the Nobel prize in economics.

Sharpe did not open his course with a formula. Mukesh remembered him starting with a question for the whole class: "how do you make a difference to the world." It is a big question for a classroom of young people who mostly want good jobs.

Mukesh had a plan for after Stanford, and it was not to go straight home. At that time, the World Bank's Young Professionals Programme was, in his words, "extremely prestigious." He planned to do that programme first and then return to work on Reliance's polyester plant.
The message from Bombay

Then the plan fell apart, in the best way. While Mukesh was at Stanford, Reliance won a government licence to make polyester itself instead of only trading it. Dhirubhai was not going to wait a year and a half for his son to finish the World Bank programme.
you are right in the way you have planned your things. I am starting work on the polyester plant.
blocks.who: Dhirubhai Ambani to Mukesh, as Mukesh recalled it in 2007

blocks.text: Notice what Dhirubhai did not say. He did not order his son home. He praised the plan and simply told him the train was leaving. Mukesh got the message: "So, I decided to come back immediately." He gave the year as ==1981==. He never finished the MBA.
Read this twice. He chose the project over the degree.

For example: waiting for the World Bank programme would have cost about 18 months. Reliance says its first petrochemicals and polyester filament yarn plant, at Patalganga, was built between 1980 and 1982 "in record time." Had he waited, most of that build would have happened without him.
His first boss was not his father

When Mukesh walked into Reliance, he did not walk into his father's office. "Rasikbhai Meswani, Nikhil and Hital's father, was my first boss," he said. Rasikbhai was running the company's polyester business.

That business was still mostly trading and processing. It imported polyester fibre, texturised it, and sold it to textile mills. Mukesh started there, learning how the existing business made money before building the new one.

Then he moved to the polyester filament yarn project. His job sounds simple on paper and is hard in real life: organise the work, set up reporting structures so everyone knew who answered to whom, and keep people motivated.
He was about 24 here. Twenty-four. Building a factory team.
Rule number one: start from zero

There was a hard rule attached to the new business. Mukesh was told to build it without borrowing people from the existing company. In his words, the instruction was: "Build this business from scratch, without taking anyone from Reliance."

That forced discipline. He had to hire, train and organise a brand new team. Mukesh later said the first 200 or so people who built Patalganga with him were still around decades later, running different businesses for the group.

Reliance also refused to cut corners on technology. It paid the American chemical giant DuPont ==$5 million== for its know-how, at a time when rivals were paying far less for their licences. Mukesh's reason was simple: "we wanted to work with the best in the world."
Getting a licence is nothing; you have to build a sustainable business.

That sentence matters because of the era. Back then, winning a government licence could feel like the finish line. __Mukesh learned that the licence only opens the door; the real work is building something that lasts.__
The big break, and a big loss

Patalganga was the start of something much larger. Reliance credits Mukesh with starting its backward integration journey: from making cloth, to making the polyester fibre that goes into cloth, to the petrochemicals that make the fibre, to refining oil, and finally to finding oil and gas.

The early years had pain too. Rasikbhai Meswani, his first boss, died on 30 August 1985. "That was a huge blow," Mukesh said. From 1985 a former public-sector manager, K. K. Malhotra, worked with Reliance for about 15 years and helped it adopt best practices, and Mukesh called him "my guru."

blocks.text: Years later, asked what his father had taught him, Mukesh gave one main rule: "always invest in businesses of the future and invest in talent." Patalganga was both. It was a bet on a new industry, and it was built by 200 new people. That is where Mukesh Ambani's real career began.

blocks.title: When the real chance arrives, the plan can change
blocks.text: Mukesh had a smart plan: Stanford, then the World Bank, then home. When the polyester licence came through, he dropped the prestigious line on his CV and went to build a factory. A plan is a tool, not a promise. If the right project appears early, being there when it starts can teach you more than any programme.

factCheck.method: Built mainly from Mukesh Ambani's own words: his 1998 Rediff interview with Pritish Nandy and his 2007 three-part MoneyLIFE interview (published on Rediff), plus Anil Ambani's 2002 interview with Vir Sanghvi for family-home details. Company facts come from Reliance's official history and chairman pages and the Forbes profile. The 2025 ICT grant was checked against ANI, Business Today and Storyboard18. The garage story is from a 2019 IBTimes India report of his Simi Garewal TV interview. Dhirubhai's background was cross-checked against Rediff (Shyamal Majumdar, 2015) and Arab News (2012). Photos were checked against the Wikimedia Commons API for author and licence. Wikipedia was used only as a lead to find sources. Live web search was rate-limited during this pass, so a few widely repeated details were dropped instead of being stated.

disputed.claim: The year the family returned from Aden to Bombay
disputed.note: Mukesh (Rediff 1998) says Dhirubhai worked in Aden 1954–1957 and came back the year Mukesh was born; Reliance's official history also says 1957. Rediff (Majumdar, 2015) says Dhirubhai returned in 1958, aged 26. The text gives both.

Mukesh himself told MoneyLIFE (2007) he came back in 1981. Many press profiles and Wikipedia say he withdrew in 1980. Reliance's official history dates the Patalganga build to 1980–82. We use his own date, 1981.

disputed.claim: Whether Mukesh holds a Stanford MBA
disputed.note: Reliance's official profile says he 'pursued an MBA from Stanford University'. Forbes lists him as a Stanford drop-out, and his own account says he left to come home before finishing. The text says he never finished the MBA.

Anil Ambani (2002) described a one-bedroom flat for seven people including their grandmother. Some later press profiles (e.g. The Weekend Leader, 2024) call it a two-bedroom apartment, and reports of the Simi Garewal interview quote Mukesh as recalling 8–9 people in one room. We follow Anil's first-hand description.

disputed.claim: Name of Dhirubhai's first trading firm
disputed.note: Arab News (2012) calls the venture with Champaklal Damani 'Majin'; Rediff (2015) calls Dhirubhai's 1958 firm Reliance Trading Corporation. The text avoids naming it.

disputed.claim: How much time Dhirubhai spent with his children
disputed.note: Mukesh (2007) recalls Sundays reserved for family and annual village camping trips; Anil (2002) said he could not recall his father spending time with him during school or college. The text presents both as personal memories.

disputed.claim: Capital Dhirubhai brought back from Aden
disputed.note: Mukesh (1998) and Rediff (2015) both say about Rs 50,000. Smaller figures that circulate online were not traced to a reliable source and were not used.
